title: Lav 2
hookLine: the second round: the Guru leads you to the fearless One, and ego's filth is gone (Suhi M4, ang 773)

lines: WILL THIS LAST? AM I ENOUGH?
cards: Will this last? Am I enough? What will his mother think?
What if we turn into our parents? Questions like these can sit under a wedding day, fear dressed up in flowers. The photos never show them.
So it's striking that the second round of the Sikh wedding, sung while the couple walks, is about fear, and about leaving it behind.

teach.h: ROUND TWO: TO MEET THE TRUE GURU.
teach.b: The second stanza of Guru Ram Das's laavan, still on Ang seven seventy-three, says, in paraphrase: in the second round, the Lord leads you to meet the true Guru.
The mind becomes nirbhau, fearless, in the fear of God, and the filth of ego is washed away. One finds the pure fear, nirmal bhau.
Singing the Lord's praises, you see the Lord everywhere, and the unstruck music sounds within. Two kinds of fear meet here. One shrinks you: what will people say, will I fail, what if I'm left.
The other, in Gurbani's language, is bhau, a reverent awe of God, like standing at the edge of an ocean.

teach.h: TWO FEARS: THE SMALL ONE AND AWE.
teach.b: In the pure fear of God, the mind becomes fearless; the awe loosens the grip of the smaller fears.

And nirbhau has come up on this path before: in the Mul Mantar, at the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, it's said of God, the Fearless One. In round two, the same word describes the mind walking toward Him.
Ego is the other thing round two names. Haumai, the I that wants to win the argument, keep score, be right.
The stanza calls it filth, and says it's washed off. For a couple, that's practical: a marriage where both stop keeping score is a different marriage.
For a soul, it's the next step after duty: once you're walking the path, the path starts to clean you. Then a lovely detail: the anahad, the unstruck sound, plays inside. A music no one is playing.

how: At the Anand Karaj, the second of Guru Ram Das's four laavan is read and then sung while the couple walks a second time around the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: fearless, free of the small fears
fear of God that makes you shrink

games.q: the second round — tap the pairs.
p: ego, washed off in round two

s: the second lav says all fear is bad
it names a pure fear of God, nirmal bhau, in which the mind becomes fearless.
nirbhau, the Fearless One, also appears in the Mul Mantar
it's among the first things the Guru Granth Sahib says about God.

games.q: you're walking the second round, worried the marriage won't last. what does the stanza set against that kind of fear?
o: a promise that nothing will go wrong.
awe of God, which loosens the smaller fears.
games.why: in the stanza, the mind becomes fearless, nirbhau, in the pure fear of God, nirmal bhau.

practice: Walk a second slow clockwise round, or trace one with your hand, carrying one small fear you have today, named plainly.

Halfway around, let your attention widen to the room, the sky outside, how much bigger the world is than the fear. Then sit and listen to whatever sound is there; if you pray, say Waheguru as you complete the round.

wordCard.voice: Nirbhau, fearless: in the second round of the Sikh wedding, led to the true Guru, awe of God replaces the small fears, ego's filth washes away, and an unstruck music plays within.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: fearless; said of God in the Mul Mantar, and of the mind in the second round.

carryVoice: Your line: round two: fearless. Awe loosens the grip of the small fears. That's day six hundred sixty-three.

sources.ref: Suhi Mahalla 4, Chhant (the laavan), second stanza, Ang 773
